title: Counting the real directions
objectives: Find the rank and use it to count the solutions of a system.
Use rank plus nullity equals the number of columns.

screens.prose: Another $3 \times 3$ matrix. Every row has non-zero entries.
screens.question: What is the rank of $\mathbf{M}$?

widget.label: Rank
widget.accept: 1: rows 2 and 3 are multiples of row 1.

hints.text: Eliminate before you count.
Compare rows 2 and 3 with row 1.
Row 2 $= -2 \times$ row 1 and row 3 $= 3 \times$ row 1. Both vanish.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run elimination, then count the pivots.

byKey.nonzero-rows: You counted the non-zero rows before eliminating. Rows 2 and 3 are multiples of row 1, so elimination wipes them out.
byKey.two: Row 3 is $3 \times$ row 1 as well, so $R_3 - 3R_1$ clears it too.

explain.text: $R_2 + 2R_1$ and $R_3 - 3R_1$ clear rows 2 and 3. One pivot is left, so the rank is 1. Every column is a multiple of $(1, -2, 3)$: $C(\mathbf{M})$ is a line.

screens.title: Full column rank
screens.prose: The $3 \times 2$ matrix from the column-space lesson has rank 2: a pivot in every column. Take $\mathbf{b} = (2, 3, 5)$, which is in $C(\mathbf{A})$.
screens.question: How many solutions are there?

options.why: No column lacks a pivot, so no variable is free. Nothing can be added to a solution.
$2 + 3 = 5$, so $\mathbf{b}$ is on the plane $z = x + y$.

hints.text: Count the free variables.
Both columns hold a pivot.
Rows 1 and 2 give $x_1 = 2$, $x_2 = 3$. Row 3 checks: $2 + 3 = 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check $\mathbf{b}$ is reachable, then count free variables.

explain.text: Rank 2 equals the number of columns, so $N(\mathbf{A}) = \{\mathbf{0}\}$. A solution exists because $\mathbf{b}$ is in $C(\mathbf{A})$, and it is unique: $\mathbf{x} = (2, 3)$. For $\mathbf{b} = (1, 1, 1)$ there would be none.

screens.title: Everything in one table
screens.prose: Three matrices you have met before. Each column of a reduced matrix holds a pivot or gives a free variable. In the last column, assume $\mathbf{b}$ is in $C(\mathbf{A})$.
screens.question: Fill in the rank, the free variables and the solutions: write one or many.

hints.text: Eliminate each matrix and count its pivots. Free variables are columns minus rank.
$\mathbf{P}$: row 2 is twice row 1. $\mathbf{R}$: row 3 vanished in the independence lesson.
Ranks 1, 2 and 2; free variables 2, 0 and 1. A free variable means infinitely many solutions.

feedback.correct: Rank plus free variables equals the columns, and free variables decide the count.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count pivots after elimination, subtract from the columns, then ask whether anything is free.

byKey.r0c3: Row 2 of $\mathbf{P}$ is twice row 1, so elimination leaves one pivot.
byKey.r2c3: $\mathbf{R}$ reduces to two non-zero rows: rank 2, though no row of $\mathbf{R}$ is zero.
byKey.r1c4: $\mathbf{Q}$ has a pivot in both columns, so nothing is free.
byKey.r1c5: $\mathbf{Q}$ has no free variable, so a reachable $\mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution.
byKey.r0c5: $\mathbf{P}$ has two free variables, so every reachable $\mathbf{b}$ has infinitely many solutions.
byKey.r2c5: $\mathbf{R}$ has a free variable, so every reachable $\mathbf{b}$ has infinitely many solutions.

explain.text: In every row, rank plus free variables is the number of columns. Each free variable gives one special solution, so the nullspace has dimension $n - r$, called the **nullity**. Nullity 0 means one solution; anything more means infinitely many.

screens.prose: For an $m \times n$ matrix of rank $r$: $$r = \dim C(\mathbf{A}) = \dim(\text{row space}), \qquad r + \dim N(\mathbf{A}) = n.$$ $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has no solution when $\mathbf{b}$ is outside $C(\mathbf{A})$. Otherwise it has one solution when $r = n$, and infinitely many when $r < n$.
screens.question: A $3 \times 5$ matrix has rank 3. How many solutions does $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ have?

options.why: Rank 3 with 5 columns leaves $5 - 3 = 2$ free variables.

options.text: None for some $\mathbf{b}$, infinitely many for others
options.why: Three pivots in three rows: $C(\mathbf{A})$ is all of 3D, so every $\mathbf{b}$ is reachable.

feedback.correct: Every $\mathbf{b}$ is reachable, and two variables are free.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the rank with the number of rows, then with the number of columns.

explain.text: Rank 3 equals the number of rows, so $C(\mathbf{A})$ is all of 3D and every $\mathbf{b}$ is reachable. Rank 3 is less than 5 columns, so two variables are free. Each $\mathbf{b}$ has infinitely many solutions.

screens.prose: Why does $r + \dim N(\mathbf{A}) = n$ always hold? Each line follows from the one before.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Each of the $n$ columns of $\mathbf{U}$ either holds a pivot or does not
$r$ columns hold pivots, by the definition of rank, so $n - r$ variables are free
Each free variable gives one special solution, and they are independent: each has a 1 where the others have 0
So $\dim N(\mathbf{A}) = n - r$, and $r + \dim N(\mathbf{A}) = n$

hints.text: Start by sorting the columns.
Count pivots before you count special solutions.
The special solutions form a basis of the nullspace, so they give its dimension.

feedback.correct: Sort the columns, count each kind, then read off the dimension.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with what every column is: pivot or free.

byKey.d3: Special solutions come from free variables, so count the free variables first.
byKey.d4: The conclusion needs the special solutions to be a basis first.

explain.text: Every column is a pivot column or a free one, so the two counts add to $n$. The special solutions are a basis of $N(\mathbf{A})$, one per free variable. So the nullspace has dimension $n - r$.

ideas: The rank $r$ is the number of pivots. It equals the dimension of the column space and of the row space.
Every column is a pivot column or a free one, so $r + \dim N(\mathbf{A}) = n$.
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has no solution if $\mathbf{b}$ is outside $C(\mathbf{A})$, one if $r = n$, and infinitely many if $r < n$.

quiz.prose: A desk has four instruments exposed to three risk factors. Its sensitivity matrix has rank 2.
quiz.question: How many independent risks can the desk hedge?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The hedgeable exposures form the column space. Its dimension is the rank.

byKey.instruments: You counted instruments. Some are combinations of others and add no new direction.
byKey.factors: You counted factors. With rank 2, one direction of factor risk is out of reach.

explain.text: The exposures the desk can create form $C(\mathbf{S})$, of dimension equal to the rank. With rank 2, two independent risks can be hedged. Exposure in the third direction cannot be offset.
